items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Gain of electrons, or a decrease in oxidation state"?
items.answer: reduction

items.stem: Why is the reaction 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl a redox reaction?
options: Sodium loses electrons and chlorine gains them.
items.answer: Sodium loses electrons and chlorine gains them.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an oxidising agent and a reducing agent.
items.answer: An oxidising agent accepts electrons and is reduced; a reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: An oxidising agent accepts electrons and is reduced; a reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidised. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: When VO₂⁺ is converted to VO²⁺, how does the oxidation state of vanadium change?
items.answer: +5 to +4, reduction
items.markingKey: A. V: +5 in VO₂⁺, +4 in VO²⁺ → reduction.

items.stem:

MnO₄⁻(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 5Fe³⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l)

(a) Calculate the amount of MnO₄⁻ in the mean titre. [1]
(b) Calculate the total amount of Fe²⁺ in the sample. [3]
(c) Calculate the percentage by mass of iron in the sample. [2]
(d) Suggest why the sample must be analysed soon after dissolving. [1]
(e) State the change in oxidation state of iron in the reaction. [1]
items.answer: (a) 3.09 × 10⁻⁴ mol (b) 0.0123 mol (c) 17.9 % (d) Fe²⁺ is slowly oxidised to Fe³⁺ by air, which would give a low result. (e) +2 to +3 (oxidised)

items.stem: Write a balanced half-equation for the oxidation of Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and combine it with MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.
items.answer: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻; MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O
items.markingKey: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻; MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O

items.stem: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) oxidises ethanol to ethanal. (a) Write the half-equation for the reduction of Cr₂O₇²⁻ to Cr³⁺. (b) Write the half-equation for the oxidation of C₂H₅OH to CH₃CHO. (c) Combine them into an overall equation. (d) State the colour change and the change in oxidation state of chromium.
items.answer: (a) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. (b) C₂H₅OH → CH₃CHO + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. (c) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3C₂H₅OH + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3CH₃CHO + 7H₂O. (d) orange to green; +6 → +3.
items.markingKey: (a) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. (b) C₂H₅OH → CH₃CHO + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. (c) Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 3C₂H₅OH + 8H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3CH₃CHO + 7H₂O. (d) orange to green; +6 → +3.

items.stem: "Half-equations represent what actually happens in a redox reaction." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They are a powerful bookkeeping model and are real in cells, but simplify the mechanism in solution.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: in electrochemical cells the half-reactions really occur at separate electrodes; they show the electron transfer clearly. Arguments against: in solution the electron transfer may be direct and via intermediates; species like "H⁺" and free electrons are simplifications. Supported judgement: They are a powerful bookkeeping model and are real in cells, but simplify the mechanism in solution. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "disproportionation".
items.answer: A redox reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced

items.stem: Explain how to balance a half-equation in acidic solution.
items.answer: Balance the element changing oxidation state, add H₂O to balance O, add H⁺ to balance H, then add electrons to balance charge.

items.stem: "The oxidising agent is the species that is oxidised." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The oxidising agent is itself reduced; it causes another species to be oxidised.
items.markingKey: The oxidising agent is itself reduced; it causes another species to be oxidised. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State the oxidation state of N in N₂O₄ and name the species using Roman numerals where appropriate.
items.markingKey: Sum of oxidation states = overall charge with O −2 (−1 in peroxides), H +1, K +1 (M1); N = +4 (A1).

items.stem: Explain why magnesium displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution.
items.answer: Magnesium is more reactive: it loses electrons more readily, reducing Cu²⁺ to Cu while being oxidised to Mg²⁺.

items.stem: "Iodine displaces chlorine from sodium chloride solution." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine and cannot oxidise Cl⁻; no reaction occurs.

items.stem: Distinguish between a redox titration and an acid–base titration.
items.answer: An acid–base titration involves proton transfer and usually needs an added indicator; a redox titration involves electron transfer and may be self-indicating.

items.stem: "Redox titrations are more useful than acid–base titrations in analysis." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Both are essential; the choice depends on whether the analyte is a redox or acid–base species.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: determine iron in tablets, ores, vitamin C, dissolved oxygen, chlorine in bleach; often self-indicating. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "electrolytic cell"?
options: An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, including electrons
A redox reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced
A species that reduces another species and is itself oxidised (an electron donor)
A cell in which electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous redox reaction
items.answer: A cell in which electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous redox reaction
items.markingKey: D. "electrolytic cell" is a cell in which electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous redox reaction.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an electrolytic cell and a voltaic cell.
items.answer: A voltaic cell uses a spontaneous reaction to produce electricity (anode −, cathode +); an electrolytic cell uses electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction (anode +, cathode −).
items.markingKey: A voltaic cell uses a spontaneous reaction to produce electricity (anode −, cathode +); an electrolytic cell uses electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction (anode +, cathode −). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why lead–acid batteries can be recharged.
items.answer: The discharge products (PbSO₄) remain on the electrodes, and an external current reverses the redox reactions to regenerate Pb and PbO₂. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Explain why E⦵ values are measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.
items.answer: The potential of a single half-cell cannot be measured alone; it must be compared with a reference half-cell whose potential is defined as zero.

items.stem: Will Ni²⁺ oxidise Cl⁻ under standard conditions? E⦵(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.26 V; E⦵(Cl₂/Cl⁻) = +1.36 V.

items.stem: Distinguish between ΔG⦵ and E⦵cell.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a reaction with a positive E⦵cell may not be observed in practice.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Standard electrode potentials reliably predict which redox reactions will occur."

items.answer: (a) 9.80 × 10⁻⁵ mol (b) 0.00490 mol (c) 11.1 % (d) Fe²⁺ is slowly oxidised to Fe³⁺ by air, which would give a low result. (e) +2 to +3 (oxidised)

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Acidified dichromate(VI) is a suitable oxidising agent for industrial alcohol oxidation."
items.answer: It is a good laboratory reagent, but greener catalytic methods are preferred industrially.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reliable, easy colour change, good yields in the laboratory. Arguments against: Cr(VI) is toxic and carcinogenic; waste disposal is costly; catalytic oxidation with air (e.g. Cu or Ag catalysts) is cheaper and greener. Supported judgement: It is a good laboratory reagent, but greener catalytic methods are preferred industrially.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "acidified potassium dichromate(VI)".
items.answer: An oxidising agent (K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) used to oxidise alcohols; it turns from orange to green as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an oxidising agent (K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) used to oxidise alcohols; it turns from orange to green as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between LiAlH₄ and NaBH₄.
items.answer: NaBH₄ is milder and can be used in water or alcohol (reduces aldehydes and ketones); LiAlH₄ is much stronger, needs dry ether and also reduces carboxylic acids.
items.markingKey: NaBH₄ is milder and can be used in water or alcohol (reduces aldehydes and ketones); LiAlH₄ is much stronger, needs dry ether and also reduces carboxylic acids. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An alcohol, warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI), turns the orange dichromate green, but the product does not react with Tollens’ reagent. Which alcohol could it be?
items.answer: pentan-3-ol
items.markingKey: A. Secondary → ketone: pentan-3-ol.

items.stem: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI). What is the organic product?
items.answer: propanoic acid
items.markingKey: C. propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol → propanoic acid.

items.stem: What is the oxidation state of sulfur in H₂SO₄?
Which term matches this description: "298 K, 100 kPa for gases and 1 mol dm⁻³ for ions in solution"?
items.answer: standard conditions (electrochemistry)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of standard conditions (electrochemistry).

items.stem: Which metal reacts with cold water to produce hydrogen?
items.answer: sodium
items.markingKey: D. Very reactive.

items.stem: Explain why fuel cells are more efficient than burning fuel to generate electricity.
items.answer: Chemical energy is converted directly to electrical energy without the heat-engine stage, which loses a large proportion as heat.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Chemical energy is converted directly to electrical energy without the heat-engine stage, which loses a large proportion as heat. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why distillation is used to obtain an aldehyde from a primary alcohol.
items.answer: The aldehyde has a lower boiling point than the alcohol (no hydrogen bonding), so it distils off as soon as it forms, preventing further oxidation to the carboxylic acid.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The aldehyde has a lower boiling point than the alcohol (no hydrogen bonding), so it distils off as soon as it forms, preventing further oxidation to the carboxylic acid. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Oxygen always has an oxidation state of −2." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Oxygen is −1 in peroxides (H₂O₂), +2 in OF₂ and 0 in O₂.
items.markingKey: Oxygen is −1 in peroxides (H₂O₂), +2 in OF₂ and 0 in O₂. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between E⦵cell and ΔG⦵.
items.answer: E⦵cell is an electrical measure (V) of the driving force – positive when spontaneous; ΔG⦵ is the energy measure (kJ mol⁻¹) – negative when spontaneous; ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵.
items.markingKey: E⦵cell is an electrical measure (V) of the driving force – positive when spontaneous; ΔG⦵ is the energy measure (kJ mol⁻¹) – negative when spontaneous; ΔG⦵ = −nFE⦵. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is the colour of the end point in a dichromate titration hard to see?
options: The change is from green Cr³⁺ to a slight orange tint, so a redox indicator is needed.
items.answer: The change is from green Cr³⁺ to a slight orange tint, so a redox indicator is needed.
items.markingKey: D. Use diphenylamine sulfonate.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a fuel cell and a rechargeable battery.
items.answer: A fuel cell needs a continuous supply of fuel and oxidant; a battery stores its reactants internally and is recharged electrically.
items.markingKey: A fuel cell needs a continuous supply of fuel and oxidant; a battery stores its reactants internally and is recharged electrically. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Write an equation for the reduction of butanal by NaBH₄ using [H].
items.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
items.markingKey: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH

items.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which is the reducing agent?
items.answer: Zn
items.markingKey: B. Cu²⁺ gains electrons (is reduced, the oxidising agent); Zn loses electrons (is oxidised, the reducing agent).

items.stem: Using E⦵(H⁺/H₂) = 0.00 V and E⦵(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.26 V, calculate the standard cell potential.
items.markingKey: D. E⦵cell = E⦵(cathode) − E⦵(anode) = 0.00 − (−0.26) = +0.26 V.

items.stem: Iodine solution is added to aqueous sodium bromide. What is observed?
options: the solution turns brown (purple in hexane)
no reaction; the colour of the added halogen remains
items.answer: no reaction; the colour of the added halogen remains
items.markingKey: D. iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than bromine.

items.stem: Molten magnesium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What is formed at the anode?
items.answer: chlorine
items.markingKey: B. Cathode: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg; anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

items.stem: Write a balanced equation, using [O] to represent the oxidising agent, for the complete oxidation of butan-1-ol and name the type of product formed.
items.answer: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + H₂O; carboxylic acid
items.markingKey: Correct product CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (1); balanced with 2[O] and H₂O (1); carboxylic acid (1).

items.stem: Deduce the oxidation states of nitrogen in NH₃, N₂, NO and NO₃⁻.
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Standard electrode potentials reliably predict which redox reactions will occur."
items.answer: They predict feasibility well under standard conditions, but kinetics and conditions determine what is actually observed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: positive E⦵cell → thermodynamically feasible; useful for predicting products and cell voltages. Arguments against: only valid under standard conditions; say nothing about rate (kinetic barriers); concentration and complexation change E. Supported judgement: They predict feasibility well under standard conditions, but kinetics and conditions determine what is actually observed.

items.stem: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell uses an alkaline electrolyte. (a) Write the half-equations at the anode and cathode. (b) Write the overall equation. (c) State the direction of electron flow. (d) Discuss one advantage and one disadvantage of fuel cells compared with lithium-ion batteries.
items.answer: (a) anode: H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻; cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. (b) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. (c) anode → cathode through the external circuit. (d) e.g. fast refuelling/only water / hydrogen storage and production.
items.markingKey: (a) anode: H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻; cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. (b) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. (c) anode → cathode through the external circuit. (d) e.g. fast refuelling/only water / hydrogen storage and production.

items.stem: Three isomeric alcohols, A, B and C, have the formula C₄H₁₀O. A is oxidised to a ketone; B is not oxidised; C gives an acid on refluxing. (a) Identify A, B and C. (b) Name the products of oxidation of A and C. (c) Describe the colour change with acidified dichromate. (d) Explain how distillation could be used to obtain an aldehyde from C.
items.answer: (a) A butan-2-ol, B 2-methylpropan-2-ol, C butan-1-ol (or 2-methylpropan-1-ol). (b) butanone; butanoic acid. (c) orange → green for A and C; stays orange for B. (d) heat with limited oxidant and distil the lower-boiling aldehyde as it forms.
items.markingKey: (a) A butan-2-ol, B 2-methylpropan-2-ol, C butan-1-ol (or 2-methylpropan-1-ol). (b) butanone; butanoic acid. (c) orange → green for A and C; stays orange for B. (d) heat with limited oxidant and distil the lower-boiling aldehyde as it forms.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "half-equation"?
options: A list of metals in order of their reactivity (ease of losing electrons to form positive ions)
An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, including electrons
NaBH₄, a reducing agent (source of hydride ions) that reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols
A connection containing an electrolyte that allows ions to move between half-cells to complete the circuit and maintain charge balance
items.answer: An equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, including electrons
items.markingKey: B. "half-equation" is an equation showing either the oxidation or the reduction part of a redox reaction, including electrons.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "standard hydrogen electrode".
items.answer: The reference half-cell, H₂(g, 100 kPa) | H⁺(aq, 1 mol dm⁻³) on platinum, assigned E⦵ = 0.00 V
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the reference half-cell, H₂(g, 100 kPa) | H⁺(aq, 1 mol dm⁻³) on platinum, assigned E⦵ = 0.00 V. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "self-indicating".
items.answer: Describes a titrant whose own colour change shows the end point, e.g. purple MnO₄⁻ becoming colourless Mn²⁺
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: describes a titrant whose own colour change shows the end point, e.g. purple MnO₄⁻ becoming colourless Mn²⁺. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims: "In all cells the anode is positive." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The anode is the site of oxidation: negative in a voltaic cell, positive in an electrolytic cell.
items.markingKey: The anode is the site of oxidation: negative in a voltaic cell, positive in an electrolytic cell. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "All alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by acidified dichromate." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only primary alcohols (via aldehydes) give acids; secondary give ketones; tertiary are not oxidised.
items.markingKey: Only primary alcohols (via aldehydes) give acids; secondary give ketones; tertiary are not oxidised. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which statement about a reducing agent is correct?
options: It donates electrons and its oxidation state increases.
items.answer: It donates electrons and its oxidation state increases.
items.markingKey: A. Reducing agent is oxidised.

items.stem: "Doubling a half-equation doubles its E⦵ value." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: E⦵ is an intensive property and does not change when the half-equation is multiplied.
items.markingKey: E⦵ is an intensive property and does not change when the half-equation is multiplied. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why starch is added only near the end point in an iodine–thiosulfate titration.
items.answer: If added when much iodine is present, a stable starch–iodine complex forms that releases iodine slowly, making the end point inaccurate.

items.stem: What happens at the anode during copper electroplating with a copper anode?
options: Copper atoms are oxidised to Cu²⁺ ions.
items.answer: Copper atoms are oxidised to Cu²⁺ ions.
items.markingKey: A. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.

items.stem: Write a balanced equation, using [O] to represent the oxidising agent, for the oxidation of butan-2-ol and name the type of product formed.
items.answer: CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₂CH₃ + H₂O; ketone
items.markingKey: Correct product CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (1); balanced with 1[O] and H₂O (1); ketone (1).

items.stem: When SO₄²⁻ is converted to SO₂, how does the oxidation state of sulfur change?
items.answer: +6 to +4, reduction
items.markingKey: C. S: +6 in SO₄²⁻, +4 in SO₂ → reduction.

items.stem: Using the E⦵ values Mn²⁺/Mn −1.18 V; H⁺/H₂ 0.00 V; Pb²⁺/Pb −0.13 V; Cl₂/Cl⁻ +1.36 V, which species is the strongest reducing agent?
items.answer: Mn
items.markingKey: A. Most negative E⦵ → Mn.

items.stem: A piece of nickel is placed in copper(II) sulfate solution. Does a displacement reaction occur?
options: Yes: hydrogen gas is produced from the copper(II) sulfate
Yes: Cu + Ni²⁺ → Cu²⁺ + Ni (balanced appropriately)
Yes: Ni + Cu²⁺ → Ni²⁺ + Cu (balanced appropriately)
items.answer: Yes: Ni + Cu²⁺ → Ni²⁺ + Cu (balanced appropriately)
items.markingKey: D. nickel is more reactive than copper.

items.stem: What are the products when copper(II) chloride solution is electrolysed?
options: copper at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
chlorine at the cathode and copper at the anode
copper at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
items.answer: copper at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
items.markingKey: A. copper(II) chloride solution: copper (cathode, most easily reduced) and chlorine (anode, most easily oxidised at that concentration).

items.stem: An alcohol, warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI), leaves the dichromate orange. Which alcohol could it be?
items.answer: 2-methylpropan-2-ol
items.markingKey: C. Tertiary – not oxidised: 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

items.stem: In the reaction 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + I₂(aq), which is the species oxidised?
items.answer: I⁻
items.markingKey: D. Fe³⁺ gains electrons (is reduced, the oxidising agent); I⁻ loses electrons (is oxidised, the reducing agent).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The activity series can be explained entirely by ionisation energies."
items.answer: IE is part of the explanation, but E⦵ values account for all the energy terms in solution.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: metals with lower IE generally lose electrons more easily. Arguments against: in water, hydration enthalpy and atomisation also matter (Li is very reactive in water despite higher IE than Cs); standard electrode potentials give a better measure. Supported judgement: IE is part of the explanation, but E⦵ values account for all the energy terms in solution. items.stem: "Hydrogen fuel cells will replace batteries in all vehicles." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Fuel cells may suit heavy transport, but batteries are likely to dominate passenger vehicles.
